content.title: About
content.content: Multigrain bread with raisins is a whole‑grain loaf that combines several cereals (wheat, rye, oats, barley) with added dried raisins. It has a dense crumb, a subtle sweetness, and the caramel‑like aroma of raisins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Multigrain bread provides more fiber and micronutrients than standard white bread.
Raisins retain many of their antioxidant compounds, such as polyphenols, even after baking.
Adding dried fruit to bread dates back to ancient Mediterranean cultures.
The blend of different grains improves the amino‑acid profile, making the loaf more nutritious.
During baking, raisins can caramelize slightly, giving the crust a golden hue.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The grains supply thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are essential for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are important for blood formation and normal muscle function.

items.title: Antioxidants from raisins
items.content: Raisins are rich in resveratrol and quercetin, which protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The combination of whole grains and raisins results in a slower rise in blood glucose compared with refined breads.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The bread contains gluten, so it should be avoided by people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Raisins add natural sugars, which may be a concern for strict low‑sugar diets.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of the oils and dried fruit, the loaf is more calorie‑dense than plain white bread.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Some grains contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption if consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the bread as a snack, for sandwiches, toast, or alongside soups and salads. It pairs well with cream cheese, nut butter, or a drizzle of honey.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the loaf in a paper bag or bread box at room temperature for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag and thaw slices as needed.

content.title: About
content.content: The chicken, bean and cheese burrito is a Mexican‑inspired dish consisting of a large soft flour tortilla filled with sautéed chicken pieces, cooked beans, melted cheese, and often rice, salsa and sour cream. It combines protein, fiber and bold flavors in a convenient handheld meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Burritos as we know them today originated in the northern United States, where Mexican cuisine merged with local ingredients.
Traditional Mexican burritos were simple, usually just beans and rice; chicken and cheese became popular in the U.S. in the 20th century.
Flour tortillas are preferred for burritos because they are more pliable than corn tortillas.
Burritos are commonly served with guacamole, adding heart‑healthy monounsaturated fats.
The United States celebrates National Burrito Day on the first Thursday of March.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken provides a complete source of high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Fiber from beans
items.content: Beans supply soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus from cheese
items.content: Cheese contributes calcium and phosphorus, nutrients important for bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken and beans are rich in B‑vitamins such as B6 and folate, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Moderate saturated fat
items.content: When made with lean chicken breast and low‑fat cheese, the burrito can be relatively low in saturated fat.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces and cheese can be high in salt; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Large burritos can be calorie‑dense due to the tortilla and cheese, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Chicken safety
items.content: Chicken must be cooked to an internal temperature of 75 °C (165 °F) to prevent salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Burritos are eaten by hand, often sliced in half. Serve with salsa, guacamole, sour cream, or fresh veggies. For a lighter option, choose a whole‑grain tortilla and reduced‑fat cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a prepared burrito in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Freeze in a separate bag at –18 °C; reheat in the microwave or oven before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Taffy is a soft, stretchy candy made from sugar, corn syrup, butter, and flavorings. It has a sweet, slightly caramel-like taste and a chewy texture. Taffy is usually sold in small bite‑size pieces, individually wrapped.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Taffy originated in the United States in the early 19th century and quickly became a popular treat.
Traditionally, taffy is pulled by hand, creating its characteristic fibrous structure.
Different countries have their own names: in the UK it’s often called “taffy,” in Japan “karēmu.”
Taffy is frequently used as an ingredient in desserts, ice cream, and baked goods.
There are many flavor variations: classic vanilla, strawberry, mint, sea‑salt caramel, and more.

items.title: Quick source of energy
items.content: The sugar in taffy is rapidly absorbed, providing an immediate boost of glucose.

items.title: Contains a small amount of fat
items.content: Butter adds a modest amount of saturated fat, which can be part of a balanced diet in moderation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Some recipes are fortified with vitamins B1, B2, and B6, supporting metabolism.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption may raise blood glucose levels and contribute to tooth decay.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Butter can trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Choking hazard for children
items.content: The soft, stretchy texture can pose a choking risk for young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Taffy can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, added to ice cream, yogurt, baked goods, or used as a decorative garnish for desserts. Keep it in a dry place to prevent stickiness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store taffy in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep it refrigerated to prevent sugar crystallization.

content.title: About
content.content: Wheat crackers are crisp baked snacks made from wheat flour, water, salt, and sometimes a small amount of vegetable oil. They are commonly enjoyed as a snack, accompaniment to soups, or as a base for sandwiches. The crackers have a light, dry texture and a neutral flavor that pairs well with a variety of toppings and dips.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Crackers originated in medieval Europe as a way to preserve bread.
Wheat crackers are often used in Italian cuisine for making breadcrumb coatings.
They can be plain or flavored with herbs, spices, and seeds.
In many countries crackers are served with hot dishes to add a crunchy element.
Low moisture content allows crackers to be stored for long periods.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Wheat crackers provide slowly digestible carbs that can help sustain fullness over time.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Traditional crackers contain virtually no fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: When made from whole‑grain wheat flour, crackers can be a good source of fiber that supports digestive health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat flour supplies thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Versatile base for nutrient‑dense meals
items.content: Crackers can be topped with protein (cheese, deli meat) and vegetables, enhancing the overall nutritional profile of a snack.

items.title: Wheat allergy or gluten intolerance
items.content: People with celiac disease or wheat allergy should avoid wheat crackers as they can trigger reactions.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Dry wheat crackers can raise blood sugar quickly, which is a consideration for individuals with diabetes.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Some varieties contain added salt; those monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt options.

items.title: Possible additives
items.content: Crackers may contain preservatives, flavor enhancers, or artificial sweeteners that not everyone tolerates.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Crackers can be eaten straight from the package, used as a base for sandwiches, added to soups and salads for crunch, or crushed and used as a breadcrumb coating for meat and fish. They also pair well with cheeses, pâtés, hummus, and vegetable dips.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store crackers in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Properly stored, they remain crisp for several months. Discard any crackers that develop a stale odor or off‑flavor.

content.title: About
content.content: The frozen mocha coffee drink, nonfat, is a refreshing cold beverage made from coffee, cocoa and low‑fat milk. It blends aromatic espresso, smooth chocolate flavor and a light creamy texture without added cream.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The drink is produced by rapid freezing, which locks in the coffee and chocolate aromas.
The nonfat version contains roughly half the calories of a traditional mocha coffee.
It often uses a natural sweetener such as stevia to reduce sugar content.
Mocha combines two popular flavors—coffee and chocolate—making it a favorite for those who enjoy both bitter and sweet notes.
The frozen format allows serving without extra ice, preserving a uniform texture.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Coffee and cocoa are rich in polyphenols, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, enhancing alertness and concentration.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: The nonfat version contains less than 0.5 g of fat per serving, suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Calcium provision
items.content: The milk base supplies calcium essential for bone health.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: Chocolate components promote serotonin production, helping improve mood.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Individuals sensitive to caffeine should limit intake to avoid anxiety or insomnia.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Low‑fat milk may trigger reactions in people allergic to lactose or casein.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Despite lower calories, the drink may contain added sugar or sweeteners, which is important for diabetics to monitor.

items.title: Cold shock
items.content: Rapid freezing can create small ice crystals; those with sensitive teeth should consume cautiously.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the frozen mocha coffee with a spoon or straw as a refreshing treat. Optional additions include a pinch of cinnamon or a dash of vanilla extract for flavor variation.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the freezer at –18 °C. After opening, consume within 2–3 days to maintain texture and flavor.

content.title: About
content.content: Hazelnuts are the edible seeds of the hazel tree (Corylus avellana), native to temperate regions of Europe and Asia. The nuts have a delicate, slightly sweet flavor and a crunchy texture. Hazelnuts are eaten raw, roasted, and are used in baking, desserts, spreads, and chocolate confections.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hazelnut belongs to the birch family and is most closely related to the walnut.
There are two main types: sweet (edible) and bitter, the latter contains cyanogenic glycosides and is not meant to be eaten raw.
Ancient Greeks and Romans already used hazelnuts in cuisine and medicine.
Hazelnuts are processed into paste (hazelnut spread), oil, flour, and flavorings for confectionery.
Hazelnut blossoms appear early in spring before the leaves unfold.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Hazelnuts are a good source of vitamin E, a powerful antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: Provides healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: The majority of fats in hazelnuts are monounsaturated, supporting heart health.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium in hazelnuts supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Provides protein and fiber
items.content: Hazelnuts supply plant protein and dietary fiber, helping to promote satiety.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Compared with many other nuts, hazelnuts contain a notable amount of calcium.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to hazelnuts, ranging up to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Hazelnuts are calorie-dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Whole hazelnuts can pose a choking risk for young children.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Hazelnuts contain oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hazelnuts can be enjoyed as a snack, added to granola, yogurt, salads, baked goods, or processed into paste and oil. Soaking or roasting softens them and makes skin removal easier. Opt for unsalted or lightly salted varieties.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store hazelnuts in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent oil rancidity. Discard nuts that smell bitter, sharp, or stale.

content.title: About
content.content: Palm hearts are the tender, heart‑shaped cores of young palm shoots. After harvesting they are usually boiled or canned. They have a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a crisp‑yet‑tender texture. Commonly used in salads, appetizers, warm dishes, and vegetarian recipes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Palm hearts are often called “tropical artichokes,” although they are unrelated to true artichokes.
They are traditionally harvested in Southeast Asia, especially Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines.
Collecting the hearts requires removing outer leaves and part of the stem, making the product a delicacy.
Canned palm hearts keep for a long time without loss of flavor or nutrients.
In some cultures they are featured in ceremonial dishes and festive feasts.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Cooked palm hearts contain about 20 kcal per 100 g, making them an excellent choice for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium aids normal heart and muscle function and helps maintain fluid balance.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2 and B6 participate in energy metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Phenolic compounds in palm hearts help combat free radicals.

items.title: Palm allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to palm hearts.

items.title: Sodium content in canned versions
items.content: Canned palm hearts often contain added salt; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium options.

items.title: Limited fresh availability
items.content: Fresh palm hearts are harvested in specific regions and may not be readily available in regular stores.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Palm hearts can be eaten cold in salads, added to vegetable stews, used as fillings for pies or vegetarian burgers. Before use they are usually rinsed and sliced. They can also be lightly sautéed with olive oil and herbs for a warm side dish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked or canned palm hearts in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. Canned versions can be kept in a cool, dry place until the expiration date on the label. Discard if an off‑odor or discoloration develops.

content.title: About
content.content: Pannetone is a traditional Italian sweet bread made from a yeasted dough enriched with raisins, candied citrus peel and often nuts. It has a light, airy crumb, a fragrant sweet flavor, and a distinctive tall, dome‑shaped appearance.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pannetone originates from Milan, where it is traditionally baked for Christmas and New Year celebrations.
Classic recipes include candied orange and lemon peel and raisins, but modern versions may contain chocolate, nuts or dried fruits.
A popular legend says a baker created pannetone as a love gift to impress his beloved.
The original recipe uses “soft” butter, which gives the cake its tender texture.
In Italy pannetone is often served with hot chocolate or sweet wine.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Provides carbohydrates and a modest amount of fat, making it a quick source of energy.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Yeast‑leavened dough contains thiamine, riboflavin and niacin, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Raisins and candied peel add fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Citrus candied peel is high in vitamin C and flavonoids, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: Compared with many sweets, pannetone typically contains little salt.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The large amount of sugar makes pannetone calorie‑dense and can raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional recipes use wheat flour, so it is unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Dried fruit sensitivity
items.content: Raisins and candied peel may cause stomach discomfort in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of butter and sugar, pannetone is fairly caloric; portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice pannetone and serve it as a dessert or snack. It can be toasted and buttered, added to yogurt, ice cream, or used in tiramisu and bread pudding recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep pannetone in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 5 days. For longer storage, refrigerate or freeze it, wrapped tightly in plastic film.
